title: The Downside of Integrity
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This post makes the counterintuitive case that integrity, a core leadership virtue, can be overdone. The problem is not too much honesty or fairness but rigidity: people use integrity to reduce complex issues to black and white, become inflexible, judge others harshly, and fear compromise. The author argues integrity must be balanced by openness to other viewpoints and by complementary strengths such as humility. The post closes with a self-check about a person known for integrity and a pointed irony that it takes integrity to admit the risk.
points: Rigidity, not dishonesty, is the failure mode of excessive integrity.
Invoking integrity can become a shortcut that flattens complexity into black and white.
Strong convictions can lead to harsh judgments of others and fear of compromise.
Other character strengths like humility are needed to balance moral standards.
quotes: We don’t normally think that someone can have too much integrity. Integrity, after all, is about acting with honesty and high standards.

People often hide behind the idea of acting with integrity to simplify a complex situation or issue. In the name of integrity, they choose to view matters in blacks and whites, overlooking the many subtleties and confounding factors that make an issue complex.
As a result of their commitment to their values, they can also become inflexible in their beliefs and decisions, and judge others harshly if they perceive them as lacking similar values.
While integrity is an essential character trait, it must be balanced with an openness to hear other viewpoints and a willingness to adapt when necessary.
Lacking other character strengths to offset inflexibility, too much integrity can render a leader incapable of seeing the delicate distinctions that make up most issues.
